analysis.one_liner: Sets national rules requiring companies to get consent before collecting your personal data, and gives you rights to see, correct, and delete it.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate on March 25, 2026 and referred to the Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors, no action, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create the first broad federal consumer privacy law. Companies would need your consent — explicit consent for sensitive data like health, biometric, and location information — before collecting your personal data. You would get rights to see what data companies hold about you, correct it, have it deleted, and take it to another company. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce it with civil penalties, backed by 440 new enforcement staff, and state attorneys general could also sue. However, it would wipe out stronger state privacy laws, give companies an implied-consent default for ordinary data, and provide no right for individuals to sue on their own.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users and consumers whose personal data — health, location, biometric, financial — is currently collected, shared, and sold with little control. Small businesses get lighter obligations, and the FTC gains staffing and penalty power. States lose some power: the bill preempts state privacy laws in favor of one federal floor.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a national baseline requiring companies to get consent before collecting personal data, with explicit opt-in consent for sensitive data like health, biometric, and precise location information.
Gives individuals rights to access their data, correct it, and have it deleted, exercisable twice a year at no charge, with data portability between companies.
Requires a comprehensive data security program and lets the FTC impose civil penalties of up to $42,530 per affected person for knowing violations.
Funds 440 additional FTC enforcement staff and lets state attorneys general sue violators directly.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that collect and monetize personal data — advertisers, data brokers, platforms, and any covered business — which would face consent requirements, deletion requests, security programs, and FTC penalties of up to $42,530 per affected person. Consumers also bear a softer cost if federal preemption wipes out stronger state privacy laws.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies that collect and sell data

drawbacks.text: The bill creates no private right of action — individuals whose data is misused cannot sue on their own; only the FTC and state attorneys general can enforce it.
Federal preemption would override stronger state privacy laws, and the bill strips the FCC of authority over data practices of companies it currently regulates.

Consent can be implied from inaction for ordinary data, and companies may decline deletion requests based on their own 'legitimate interests,' giving consumers less control than the bill's headline suggests.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real but constrained: enforcement is left entirely to the FTC and state attorneys general, with no private right of action, and the federal floor would override stronger state privacy laws while also stripping the FCC of its role over data held by telecom companies. The 440-person FTC enforcement office would need to police thousands of companies. Weighed honestly: meaningful national privacy rights at the cost of a weaker enforcement toolkit and possibly weaker rules in states that had set a higher bar.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has taken no action, and no senator has signed on to support it.

narrative.text: Introduced March 25, 2026 and immediately referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
Zero cosponsors as of the available record.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo: companies continue collecting and selling personal data under current rules, and stronger state privacy laws remain the only protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data companies and ad platforms, for now

for.name: Sen. Jerry Moran
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Commerce Committee, where it has received no further action and no cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: With a single sponsor and no cosponsors, votes, or public opposition recorded, no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Data brokers, ad-tech, and online platforms that monetize personal data
industries.note: New consent, deletion, and security duties with per-person civil penalties of up to $42,530 and 440 new FTC enforcers. In exchange, federal preemption replaces a patchwork of state privacy laws with one national rule.
Exempt from the access and correction rights and given lighter-touch compliance, but still bound by core collection and security rules.
Covered by the FTC's privacy enforcement for the first time, but the bill removes the FCC's authority over their data practices.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors a month-plus in and no committee activity, the bill is very unlikely to advance; most bills referred to committee never receive a hearing or vote, and it will die at the end of the 119th Congress unless it gains co-sponsorship and committee attention.
